title: Architecture and components
summary:
This part settles RichView's architecture for the rewrite: layers and dependency direction, where product behaviour lives, safety boundaries, workspace topology, publishing and deployment, and one keep/change/drop card for every component on `main`, on the open draft PRs and in the lockdown tooling. Feature behaviour (04), field types (05), styles (06) and budgets (07) are out of scope; cards point there when a detail belongs elsewhere.

Key decisions:

- **Pure core, Rust everywhere** (ARC-02, ARC-03, ARC-68): core and engine never touch I/O; handwritten JavaScript only in named adapters, a narrow landing animation layer and development tooling that never ships; every dependency passes a licence gate.
- **Two Wasm runtimes; reports embed theirs** (ARC-06, ARC-07, ARC-17): 87% of a small chart report is the shared runtime, which also carries the site, and outside the checkout the CLI cannot export chart reports. ARC-06 also answers PRF-31's shared hosted runtime.
- **Safety boundaries** (ARC-10 to ARC-15, ARC-23, ARC-66): with sleek or sleek-dark in the cascade a style file injects `<script>` into reports today, no host on `main` sends a Content Security Policy, the MCP publish tool takes the token as an argument, and the playground loads sources from any CORS-enabled URL.
- **Publishing and deployment** (ARC-20 to ARC-22, ARC-57): one publish contract with server-side rendering, immutable versions, richview.ai as a static site with a `dev` preview behind Cloudflare Access, and RichView's paid hosted services: hosted Cowork at app.richview.ai, Publish servers for customers and hosting for large data and media; Publish rebuilt in the rewrite on a server core shared with Cowork, and News on #70's code, merged into `main`, until it moves onto it.
- **One workspace** (ARC-16 to ARC-19): INT-50 keeps one repository; publication content gets its own repository, `richview-web` splits into report and site crates, chart geometry stays inside `richview-chart`, and `.rmd` blocks are the only chart contract.

Where another part owns a decision, the card here states the component consequence and cites the owner instead of asking again: INT-50 (repository), INT-52 (Rust), INT-53 (chart supplier), INT-71 (installation), INT-74 (News), TYP-32 (embed diagnostic level), TYP-51 (style sinks), TYP-63, TYP-64, TYP-95 and TYP-96 (republish, retention, content identity, latest), FEA-RP-14 (raw HTML), FEA-RP-43 (PDF bar), FEA-SF-01, FEA-SF-09, FEA-SF-15, FEA-SF-17, FEA-SF-20, FEA-SF-21 and FEA-SF-45 (commands, MCP tools, report list, render API, server binary, extension delivery, reel), DEL-39 (hosted CI), DEL-46 (agent instructions) and OPN-08, OPN-09, OPN-10, OPN-12 and OPN-14 (PR dispositions). Changing one of those answers changes the cards that cite it; pairs that still disagree are recorded under each card's conflicts.

On component cards, keep means the component and its responsibility stay in the architecture; whether its code is ported or rewritten follows INT-49. ARC-25 to ARC-56 and ARC-62 to ARC-64 cover `main`; ARC-65 covers the lockdown tooling that DEL-45 merges first into `dev`; ARC-57 covers #70, merged into `main` on 2026-10-26, and ARC-58 to ARC-61 cover components that exist only on open draft PRs. Linear's component labels in `evidence/linear.md` are aliases, not lockdown IDs: C-RICH-MARKDOWN, C-THEMES and C-RENDERER are ARC-26; C-CHART-ENGINE is ARC-25; C-SERVER is ARC-31 with ARC-32; C-CLI-MCP is ARC-28 with ARC-33; C-VSCODE is ARC-45; C-PUBLISH is ARC-57; C-DASHBOARDS is ARC-58; C-WEBSITE is ARC-38 to ARC-43 and ARC-55, with ARC-64 for the chart-review pages.

How to answer: **accept** keeps the proposal as written; **edit** replaces it with your text; **reject** drops the proposal from the rewrite (add a note with what you want instead); **defer** leaves it open. Part 08's cross-part contradiction cards (OPN-50 to OPN-68) decide conflicts involving this part's cards and should be answered first.

items.title: Layers and dependency direction
items.question: Is the rewrite organised in the layers below, with dependencies pointing only downwards?
items.why: Fixes which crate may depend on which and where each new capability lands. Today the editor, build and bench crates depend on the whole native app, and site code ships inside the runtime every chart report embeds.
items.proposed:
| Layer | Components | May depend on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Engine | `richview-chart` | no RichView crate |
| Core | `richview-core`: format, validation, styles, renderer, knowledge | Engine |
| Host services | resolver, export, store, browser host service for PDF and measurement (native) | Core, Engine |
| Hosts | CLI, HTTP host, MCP; editor service; report runtime and site runtime (Wasm) | Host services (native hosts only), Core, Engine |
| Adapters | VS Code extension, Cloudflare Workers, generated JavaScript glue | one host or runtime |
| Content and tools | site pages, docs, examples, build, bench, verification scripts, benchmark labs, font pipeline, lockdown app | any layer; nothing depends on them |

The five public elements map onto the layers: Rich Markdown and themes are core, the engine is `richview-chart` plus core's renderer, the server is a host, and the editor is the editor service plus the VS Code adapter.

**Interfaces between the layers** (Daniel, 29 Oct 2026, relayed by the chief of staff; waiting for his confirmation in the app). Each layer exposes a narrow, tested interface, and everything else is `pub(crate)` behind it:
- chart-type registration lives in `richview-chart`, so adding a chart type touches the engine only;
- one chart payload module, with a contract test for encoding and decoding, is the only format between core and the report runtime;
- a chart facade in `richview-chart` and a document API in `richview-core` are what other crates call;
- public-API snapshots of each crate and a dependency-rule check that enforces the table above run in the fast gate, so a change to an interface or a layer edge is visible in review.

options.label: Layers, downward only
options.detail: Clear ownership, enforceable by Cargo dependencies; needs the runtime split (ARC-06) and a narrower dependency for editor, build and bench (ARC-27).

options.label: Keep today's crate graph
options.detail: No restructuring; editor, build and bench keep compiling the server, MCP, PDF and S3 code, and every report keeps carrying site code.

items.recommendation: Layers, downward only. The Rust brief asked for "one shared Rust core and the smallest useful public interfaces", and this makes ARC-06 and ARC-27 checkable by `cargo` rather than by review.

items.title: Core and engine are pure
items.question: Do the `richview-core` and `richview-chart` libraries stay free of filesystem, network, process, environment and clock access, with every input resolved by a host?
items.why: Decides whether one core can run natively, in Wasm, in the editor and in Workers with identical output, and keeps every trust decision in the resolver (ARC-10).
items.proposed: The `richview-core` and `richview-chart` libraries perform no filesystem, network, process, environment or clock access. Hosts resolve styles, data, media and font catalogs into typed render options; core never receives a path or URL to load. Host-only state (`_renderHeight`, `_xWindow`, `_csvNumericText`, `_facetColorScope`) travels in typed options outside the document, so source cannot set it (D-TYP-INTERNAL-KEYS, TYP-11). Command-line tools live outside the library crates. A gate fails if either library gains an I/O-capable dependency or uses `std::fs`, `std::net`, `std::process` or `std::env`.

items.title: Where JavaScript is allowed
items.question: Where exactly may handwritten JavaScript exist, given that Rust owns all product behaviour?
items.why: INT-52 (part 01) keeps RichView in Rust and leaves the exact JavaScript boundary to this part. The answer decides whether siblings such as Publish and Dashboards may keep product logic in JavaScript, what reviews must reject and what counts as tooling. On `main`, product JavaScript is the 326-line VS Code adapter and the 65-line signup Worker, whose consent and validation rules exist only in JavaScript; tooling adds 60 Node and TypeScript files and eight Python scripts in `scripts/`, Node, Python and R harnesses in `benchmarks/` and 29 evidence scripts in `docs/evidence/`. PR #70, merged into `main` as it is on 2026-10-26 (97ac0d0, INT-52), added about 4,000 lines of JavaScript.

options.label: Rust plus thin adapters
options.detail: One implementation of every rule; Workers carry a Wasm module and a thin router. Publish's 2,329 lines of Worker and editor JavaScript, merged as they are (INT-52), are ported when the rewrite reaches Publish, and the 65-line signup Worker gains a Wasm build.

options.label: Thin adapters, small self-contained Workers in JavaScript
options.detail: The signup endpoint keeps its 65 lines because no Rust code shares its rules; contradicts INT-52's "No product rule exists only in JavaScript".

options.label: Allow JavaScript product layers in siblings
options.detail: Faster for Publish and Dashboards; access, editorial and rendering-adjacent rules exist twice, which the Rust brief ruled out.

items.recommendation: Rust plus thin adapters. The 2026-10-04 brief made it a hard constraint ("Rust owns all first-party product behavior"), and the single-implementation benefit only holds if siblings follow it.

items.title: Wasm boundary and build profile
items.question: Is every Wasm module built with wasm-bindgen at one pinned version and one size-oriented profile, with the raw `rv_*` exports removed?
items.why: Decides the one boundary every page and report uses, and which runtime bytes a commit produces. Today the shipped module carries two boundaries, wasm-bindgen plus raw C ABI exports that nothing calls, and two documented build profiles produce different bytes for the same commit.
items.proposed: Browser and Worker modules use wasm-bindgen, pinned in `Cargo.lock` (0.2.129 today) and checked against the installed CLI by the build. Each module exposes one generated API (ARC-36); handwritten `extern "C"` exports such as `rv_alloc` and `rv_frame`, and the engine's `cdylib` crate type that exists for them, are removed. Every Wasm build uses one profile: `opt-level = "s"`, LTO, one codegen unit. Native binaries keep `opt-level = 3`. The build manifest records profile and runtime hashes (ARC-46). Changing the Wasm profile is a performance decision backed by before/after numbers (part 07).

options.label: wasm-bindgen only
options.detail: Typed glue for browsers, Node and Workers; already the working boundary for every page and report.

options.label: Raw C ABI exports
options.detail: No generated glue; strings and handles cross by hand and need handwritten JavaScript, which ARC-03 forbids outside adapters.

options.label: Wasm component model
options.detail: Typed, language-neutral interfaces; browsers need a transpile step, so it adds tooling without removing glue (inferred).

items.recommendation: wasm-bindgen only. The raw exports have no caller in the repository, and one profile keeps runtime hashes comparable across builds.

items.title: Static-first SVG with Wasm hydration
items.question: Do charts render with WebGL by default from the engine's geometry model, with vector output only for PDF export, and what does a reader without JavaScript or WebGL see in place of a chart?
items.why: Fixes what a report shows without scripts (print, PDF, blocked JavaScript, feed readers) and rules canvas or raster-first rendering in or out.
items.proposed:
Charts render with WebGL by default (Daniel's INT-31 answer, 2026-10-26). The report runtime draws every chart from the engine's geometry model (ARC-18) into a WebGL canvas, and hover, zoom, keyboard access, table view, chart actions and motion work on that drawing. There is no static SVG first render by default. Before the runtime starts, each figure already holds its final box, sized from the geometry model's aspect ratio, with its title, subtitle, caption and source note in HTML, so mounting the canvas moves nothing (PRF-35). Only PDF export converts charts to vector output: it draws each chart through the engine's vector renderer from the same model at its print width, and it may take time (FEA-RP-43, PRF-16). Checks measure the geometry model, not a browser's SVG (INT-18, FEA-CH-58).

Open questions for Daniel, not decided here:

- **Readers without JavaScript or WebGL** (scripts blocked, feed readers, WebGL disabled, unsupported or lost): what stands in for a chart; options below. FEA-RP-39, INT-07, DEL-57, FEA-CH-64 and PRF-38 follow the answer.
- **Text and labels**: drawn in WebGL from the bundled fonts, or laid over the canvas as HTML or SVG text (FEA-CH-30).
- **Accessibility**: how screen-reader and keyboard users reach marks that a canvas does not expose: a generated ARIA layer, the Table, or both (FEA-CH-55).
- **WebGL in the offline file and the VS Code preview**: whether the renderer runs in a file opened from disk and in the VS Code webview on every platform and browser RichView supports; not proven yet (FEA-RP-38, FEA-SF-23, FEA-RP-59).
- **WebGL stack**: raw WebGL2 from Rust/Wasm, `wgpu`, or another (ARC-18).
- **Runtime size**: what the WebGL renderer adds to the report runtime (PRF-31).

options.label: Vector snapshot generated at export
options.detail: Each chart's vector render is inlined in the HTML and the canvas replaces it; readable and sharp without scripts, closest to today, but every report carries a second drawing of every chart, and vector conversion runs on every export, not only for PDF, which goes beyond INT-31's wording.

options.label: Static image generated at export
options.detail: A raster image per chart, drawn natively from the vector render at the figure widths; readable without scripts, but each report grows by one image per chart and width, and its text is neither selectable nor sharp when zoomed.

options.label: Data table
options.detail: Without the runtime each chart shows its source rows as an HTML table (FEA-CH-45) under its title and caption; small, accessible and exact, but no picture of the chart.

options.label: Frame and notice only
options.detail: The figure keeps its title, caption and a one-line notice that the chart needs JavaScript and WebGL; smallest, but the chart's content is out of reach without them.

items.recommendation: Open for Daniel. INT-31 settles WebGL as the default; whether readers without JavaScript or WebGL get a fallback, and which, is his call.

Daniel's INT-31 answer replaces this card's earlier proposal, static-first SVG with Wasm hydration and SVG as the canonical output, and settles June dec-49 (no canvas) the other way: WebGL is the default, not an opt-in acceleration (OPN-39, FEA-CH-47). Cards written for SVG first change with it: FEA-RP-39 and INT-07 promised static charts without scripts, FEA-CH-64 and PRF-38 size and judge static frames that exist only if a snapshot fallback is chosen, DEL-57 expected every chart as static SVG, and FEA-CH-46's in-browser SVG download goes beyond “only PDF export converts to vector”. The renderer therefore needs a shared context or must release off-screen charts (ARC-18), and every reader path needs an answer to the fallback question above.

items.title: Report and site runtimes, and how reports load them
items.question: Do reports use a report-only Wasm runtime, separate from the site runtime, embedded in every exported report, linked from the host for hosted reports, with trusted previews linking their host's copy?
items.why: Decides report size, how the runtime budget is shared and whether a report depends on a host. Every chart report carries the whole site today: in a three-block report of 2,314,593 bytes, the embedded runtime is 2,016,716 bytes (87%), and the delivered Wasm uses 96.6% of its 1.5 MiB gzip budget. Previews already link a runtime instead of embedding it: the VS Code preview loads the extension's copy, and the playground and landing demo load the site's copy through `runtime_url`, which source cannot set. PRF-31 (part 07) lists a shared runtime for hosted reports as an option; this card owns that choice and leaves part 07 the byte budgets.
items.proposed:
Two Wasm modules are built from one workspace:

- **Report runtime**: the WebGL chart renderer and chart interaction (ARC-05, ARC-18), table sorting, chart actions, theme switching, the settle hook `window.__richview` and, if FEA-CH-59 keeps it, browser glyph measurement. It carries no parser, Markdown, YAML, sanitizer, validator, knowledge bundle or site code.
- **Site runtime**: playground authoring (parse, validate, render, check) and source buffer, landing and homepage motion, showcase controls, docs gallery helpers. Site pages load it; reports never do.

Exported files embed the report runtime, so every exported report opens offline (INT-04). A report host serves stored reports small: it links the report runtime from one content-hashed, immutably cached URL on the same host, automatically when it stores a report, and keeps every runtime version a stored report links (ARC-21, PRF-31). The self-contained file stays downloadable from the host (INT-04). Trusted previews link their host's copy of the report runtime by URL, as today: the VS Code preview uses the extension's copy, the playground and landing demo the site's copy; source never selects runtime code. PDF export prints the report rendered for PDF, whose charts are the engine's vector output, so it needs no WebGL (FEA-RP-43); browser checks use the report runtime. Each module has its own size budget in part 07 (PRF-31 for the report runtime, PRF-30 for the site runtime). A gate fails if the report runtime links site modules.

options.label: Two modules, embedded in reports
options.detail: Smaller reports, independent budgets and every report self-contained; two builds and two generated APIs, and each report still carries its runtime.

options.label: Two modules, shared URL when hosted (PRF-31)
options.detail: Hosted readers download the runtime once and reuse it across reports; stored reports depend on the host keeping every runtime version, and served HTML differs from the exported file.

options.label: One module (current)
options.detail: One build; every report keeps paying for site code, and site growth consumes the report budget.

items.recommendation: Two modules, shared URL when hosted: Daniel's INT-04 answer (2026-10-26) makes reports self-contained by default and small when served from a server; exports keep embedding.

items.title: The CLI carries its own report runtime
items.question: Does the `richview` binary embed the report runtime, so a chart report exports self-contained from any directory?
items.why: Decides whether exports work from any directory. Native builds already compile the font catalogs in, but the binary looks for the runtime at run time: `RICHVIEW_PUBLIC_DIR`, then `dist/web` under the current directory, then a `share/richview/web` or `public` folder beside the binary. Anywhere else a chart report fails with `report.output.runtime`, while the app README promises a static fallback.
items.proposed: The `richview` binary embeds the report runtime (ARC-06) at build time, as it already embeds the font catalogs, so exports are self-contained from any working directory. A build without the runtime fails; it never silently ships reports whose charts show only their frame and notice (G-NO-SILENT-NOOP, INT-64, ARC-05). No flag or environment variable selects a runtime from disk, and `--public-dir` leaves every command (FEA-SF-01). The build manifest (ARC-46) records the embedded runtime hash, and the binary reports it (for example in `richview --version`). Only the report host (`richview server`, FEA-SF-20) produces the hosted page that links the runtime and fonts from its content-hashed routes (INT-04, ARC-24); the CLI's `generate`, export and PDF always produce the self-contained file, and no flag switches them to linked output.

options.detail: Self-contained installs and one versioned artifact; the binary grows by about 1.5 MB.

options.detail: Smaller binary; fails outside the checkout or install layout, and runtime and binary can drift apart.

options.label: Static fallback when missing
options.detail: Never fails; silently ships every chart as its frame and notice, since ARC-05 builds no static chart, which the current test forbids.

items.recommendation: Embed in the binary: one binary, one runtime hash, no dependence on the working directory.

items.title: One operation layer behind every surface
items.question: Are validate, check, render and the publish request implemented once in core, with export and publish as host services and the CLI, MCP, HTTP, editor and Wasm surfaces as thin transports over the same functions and diagnostics?
items.why: Decides whether every surface gives the same answer for the same source. Surfaces disagree today: a bar chart whose encodings name missing fields is `clean` in `richview check` and passes `validate`, while the editor reports an `authoring.field` error; `validate` returns `ok` but `check` has no `ok` key.
items.proposed: Core exposes one function per operation (validate, check, render, build publish request), each returning one result type with the diagnostics contract `{level, code, message, path, line?, tag?, details?}`. Every rule, including field existence and required channels, lives in core. Export (HTML file, PDF) and publishing are host services built on these operations (ARC-01, ARC-29, ARC-30). A surface only decodes its input, calls the operation and encodes the result; it adds no rules and drops no diagnostics. Machine-readable outputs share one envelope across operations, including `ok`. Native and Wasm builds of one commit return identical diagnostics and byte-identical HTML, chart geometry models and vector output for identical inputs, extending FEA-RP-01 across targets. A contract test runs every fixture through CLI, MCP, HTTP, editor and Wasm and compares diagnostics and output. items.title: Supported platforms
items.question: Which operating systems and architectures do the CLI, report server, editor service and extension support?
items.why: No card said, yet several depend on it: the extension ships a native `richview-editor` per platform (FEA-SF-21 proposes `darwin-arm64` and `linux-x64`), PDF export runs only on macOS and Linux, the gate runs only on Claw Mini, a macOS arm64 host (DEL-22), hosted CI would run on Linux x64 (DEL-39), the container is Debian Linux, and the only prerelease shipped a Linux x64 CLI. INT-71 installs RichView through an install script, builds from `prod`, the extension listings and a source build. Since 18 Nov 2026 Windows x64 ships: 3.0.0-alpha.2 carried it as a preview without PDF or SQL, and Daniel asked the same day for Windows to work end to end.
items.proposed: RichView supports macOS on arm64, Linux on x64, and Windows 10 and 11 on x64 (`x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`), with the same features on each: the CLI with its local preview, the MCP server, the editor service for the extension, PDF output through a local Chromium-family browser (Microsoft Edge comes with Windows) and SQL data sources. On Windows the SQL worker is confined as on Linux: a restricted token whose only restricting SID is new for each launch, Untrusted integrity, no privileges, and a one-process job. As on Linux and macOS, DuckDB opens the declared source only inside that confinement. Once per render the host copies the source's bytes, unparsed, into a new folder in the temporary folder that only the running launch's SID may read. It refuses a source over 4 GiB, one that would leave less than 1 GiB free there, and a temporary folder on a network share or named by volume GUID, and the next render sweeps the copies a killed render left. On every platform the worker may read the database file alone, so a database whose last changes are still in its `.wal` file is refused until a writer has written them into it. The restricted token can open nothing by path, so before it restricts itself the worker takes a handle to that folder, and its opens of files in that folder, and only those, go through the handle; every other path reaches Windows unchanged and is refused, and the restricted token decides every open. Its probe shows no file, network (socket creation through the network driver included) or process reach beyond the Linux sandbox's. The gate proves macOS on Claw Mini (DEL-22); Linux x64 is proven by the container build and by hosted CI when it runs (DEL-39). Windows is proven for each candidate by the recorded end-to-end walk on a fresh AWS Windows Server 2025 machine (`tools/windows-e2e`); Windows 10 and 11 share its kernel and are expected to behave the same, but stay untested because AWS offers no Windows 11 image. The walk covers: install with the PowerShell one-liner, `init`, edit, `check` and `generate`, the local preview, the editor service, PDF, SQL with a hostile query, the MCP server, publish to a RichView server and open it, upgrade from the previous release, and uninstall. `merge-prod` refuses a candidate that ships Windows without that walk passing on its exact commit. The Windows programs are not signed until Daniel buys a certificate. Other targets may build from source (INT-71) but carry no promise. A platform is added only together with a gate that runs on it.

items.title: Hosts never fetch report inputs
items.question: Do RichView hosts never fetch remote data, styles or media while rendering, so renders read only local, verified files?
items.why: Decides whether renders depend on the network. The CLI and docs advertise `--allow-network` with DNS-pinned HTTPS loading, but the parameter has been ignored since PR #15 (2026-10-05); agents are promised a capability that does not exist. Daniel's INT-31 answer puts author-hosted assets and RichView-managed hosting in the rewrite (TYP-41, ARC-34), so hosted assets need a path that keeps renders offline.
items.proposed:
No native or server host fetches report inputs over the network while rendering or checking. Remote data, styles and media are saved into the report folder before rendering. The one exception is a block's URL data source: the reader's browser downloads it when the report opens, never a render or check, so its data follows what the URL serves, with no warning (OPN-63). `--allow-network` and its documentation are removed (TYP-39). TYP-40 (part 05) makes a plain remote media URL an error, except a photo hotlinked from `images.unsplash.com` with its credit, which the reader's browser loads as FEA-RP-62 (accepted) builds it; `richview image search` and `use` call Unsplash only when the author runs them, never during a render or check. Hosted assets, on RichView's managed hosting or the author's own host, enter a report only as integrity-pinned asset references (D-TYP-ASSET-REF, TYP-41): renders and checks read the verified local copy the upload keeps, and an explicit download command, never a render, fetches and verifies a missing copy (ARC-34). A published page links hosted assets and the reader's browser loads them; a dataset is checked against its SHA-256 before use. Embeds (ARC-14) stay the only other remote content. A SQL source resolves on a RichView server through its connectors, never in the reader's browser (OPN-63). The playground's source loading is ARC-66.

Open: what the self-contained HTML file and the PDF hold for a hosted asset (a link, a poster or placeholder, or the bytes below a size limit), since INT-04 makes self-contained the default (TYP-42); and how a server that re-renders on publish (ARC-20) renders a block whose data is hosted: the publish request carries the verified copy, or the block draws in the reader's browser; and what a render draws and checks for a block whose data comes from a URL, before the reader's browser has fetched it.

options.detail: Renders stay deterministic and offline, with no server-side request forgery surface; hosted assets reach readers by link, verified by hash.

options.label: Opt-in DNS-pinned HTTPS (as documented)
options.detail: Convenient for agents; reintroduces fetch timeouts, SSRF risk and non-reproducible renders, and the fetch code PR #15 removed would have to be rebuilt.

options.label: No remote assets at all
options.detail: The earlier proposal; contradicts INT-31, which puts uploads and managed hosting in the rewrite.

items.recommendation: No render-time fetch; pinned references from a local copy: renders stay reproducible and free of request-forgery risk, and hosted assets still reach readers.

items.title: Content Security Policy and report origin
items.question: Do report-serving hosts and exported reports carry a strict Content Security Policy, with a separate report origin required once a host has sessions or private reads?
items.why: Decides what a script escape can reach. No RichView host on `main` sends a CSP, and the native host serves reports on the same origin as its API and, today, the site (ARC-24 removes the site); ARC-12 shows an escape exists. The Publish gateway on PR #70 already sends a CSP.
items.proposed: Every host that serves reports sends a CSP: `default-src 'none'`; scripts only by hash of the embedded report runtime, or on a report host by the host's own content-hashed runtime URL with an integrity hash (INT-04, ARC-06), plus `'wasm-unsafe-eval'`; the renderer's inline styles; fonts, images and media from `data:`, `blob:` and the report origin, and images also from `images.unsplash.com` for hotlinked Unsplash photos (FEA-RP-62); frames only from the embed allowlist; network requests (`connect-src`) only to the URLs the report's URL data sources declare, and none otherwise (OPN-63); `base-uri 'none'`; `frame-ancestors` set per host. Exported reports carry the same policy in a `<meta>` tag so it also applies when opened from disk. Previews that link their host's runtime copy (ARC-06) allow that script by its origin and an integrity hash. Publishing clients authenticate to a report host with bearer tokens, and the host serves no site pages (ARC-24). Every RichView server gets sign-in and private reads from its first cut (FEA-SF-19), so user reports are served from a dedicated report origin before read protection ships, the same hosted, in a container or self-hosted. `X-Content-Type-Options` and `Referrer-Policy` stay on every response.

items.title: Chart rendering stays inside the engine
items.question: Is `richview-chart` the only code that computes chart geometry, with one geometry model drawn by a WebGL renderer on the page and a vector renderer for PDF, and Highcharts and ECharts only as local benchmarks?
items.why: INT-53 (part 01) keeps RichView's own engine, rules out third-party renderers and closes S27-410; this card fixes the architectural consequence of ending the project's longest-running reversal (history under conflicts).
items.proposed:
`richview-chart` is the only code that computes chart geometry: from a validated chart, resolved rows, width and style it produces one geometry model per chart (scales, marks, labels, annotations and their boxes), which every renderer draws and every check measures (INT-18, FEA-CH-58). Two renderers draw that model: a WebGL renderer, the default on every page (Daniel's INT-31 answer), and a vector renderer that PDF export and the server's link-preview thumbnails use (FEA-RP-43, ARC-69) and that may be slow. The engine stays pure (ARC-02): the model and the vector renderer live in the engine crate, and the WebGL calls live in the report runtime (ARC-35), which draws the model it is given and adds no geometry of its own. Because browsers cap live WebGL contexts per page (ARC-05), the renderer shares contexts across charts or releases off-screen ones, and redraws from the model after a lost context; a chart it cannot draw shows ARC-05's notice in its frame. No third-party chart library is shipped, vendored or loaded at runtime; Highcharts and ECharts run only locally, outside the product build, as visual and behavioural benchmarks (ARC-64).

Open question for Daniel: the WebGL stack. Daniel's ARC-05 answer sets the bar it is judged on: very high performance with many points, in recent Safari, Firefox and Chrome. Options, none measured here: raw WebGL2 calls from Rust through `web-sys`, the thinnest layer, with shaders written by hand; `wgpu`, a portable GPU layer with a WebGL2 backend today and WebGPU later, which brings its own abstraction and shader translation into the runtime; or a JavaScript WebGL library, which Daniel's INT-52 answer (Rust and WebAssembly for speed; JavaScript only where ARC-03 allows) argues against and which would need an entry in ARC-03's allowlist. PRF-31 measures what each adds to the report runtime.

items.question: Is a published report an immutable `{slug, version}` record that stores its inputs and rendered HTML, with re-rendering only as a comparison?

Re-rendering with a newer engine is a comparison tool (FEA-SF-16) and never replaces the stored artifact. items.title: Link-preview thumbnails are rendered by the server core
items.question: Which component renders the link-preview thumbnail of every story with an address, when, from what, and where is it stored and served?
items.why: Daniel's INT-07 answer gives every story with an address a designed thumbnail in its own style, with its title, wherever its link is shared: like the card a shared song gets (FEA-SF-55, FEA-RP-51). FEA-SF-55 says the host renders it when the story is published or changed, but no architecture card says which component draws it, from what, or where it is kept. ARC-05 builds no snapshot inside the page, a server may have no GPU for WebGL, and PDF export (ARC-30) needs a local Chromium that a Cowork container may not carry.
items.proposed: The server core (INT-35, INT-83), which Cowork and Publish share, renders each version's thumbnail when it stores the version (ARC-20), as a 1200×630 PNG with the content FEA-SF-55 describes: the story's title and byline set in its own style over its lead chart, or its cover image (FEA-RP-62) when it has no chart. A cover that is a report-local or pinned image is drawn from the stored bytes. A cover that is a hotlinked Unsplash photo is not fetched: the render makes no network request (ARC-11), so a story whose only picture is an Unsplash cover gets the title card without it, and an og:image never shows an uncredited photo. The lead chart is drawn from the engine's geometry model by the vector renderer that PDF export also uses (ARC-18) and rasterized natively in Rust, so no WebGL and no browser are needed and the result is the same hosted, in a container or self-hosted. Text uses the style's bundled faces (ARC-62). The thumbnail belongs to the immutable stored version (ARC-21): re-rendering with a newer engine never replaces it, so a shared link keeps its preview. The host serves it from a versioned route beside the story (ARC-24, ARC-31), under the story's own access rule: a story shared only with signed-in readers has a thumbnail only they can fetch, so a link preview never reveals a private story (Daniel's INT-07 answer, OPN-54), and `og:image` points at that route (FEA-RP-51). The card is the same for a private, missing or deleted story in status, headers and bytes, so an anonymous request cannot tell them apart (FEA-SF-55, FEA-SF-64). `richview serve` renders the same thumbnail on demand and offers it at `/thumbnail` (FEA-SF-08), so an author can check what a chat will show before publishing, while the served page carries no `og:` tags (FEA-RP-51). A story whose lead chart cannot be drawn gets the title card without it. items.title: Publish and upload credentials stay out of source and agent context
items.question: Do publish tokens and upload credentials come only from the host environment, an explicit CLI flag or editor secret storage, never from report files or MCP tool arguments?
items.why: Decides where a publishing or upload secret can leak. The MCP `richview_publish` tool lists `token` as an argument (with an environment fallback), which invites agents to paste the secret into their context, transcripts and logs; the CLI and VS Code already keep it out of report files. Daniel's INT-31 answer adds uploads to RichView's managed hosting and to authors' own stores, a second secret of the same kind (INT-79).
items.proposed: A publish token is read only from the host environment, an explicit `--token` flag or VS Code secret storage per server. It is never read from `.rmd`, styles, frontmatter or MCP tool arguments; the MCP publish tool uses the token configured in its host environment. Tokens travel only over HTTPS (plain HTTP to loopback only), never across redirects, and are redacted from every error, log and diagnostic. A report host compares tokens in constant time and refuses publishing when no token is configured. Upload credentials for RichView's managed hosting or an author's own store (ARC-34) follow the same rules: read only from the host environment, an explicit flag or editor secret storage, never from report files or MCP tool arguments, sent only over HTTPS and redacted everywhere. Data-source credentials for connectors follow the same rules: they live only in the configuration of the RichView server that offers the connector, Cowork or Publish, local or hosted, and never appear in `.rmd` files, styles, report folders, rendered output, MCP tool arguments or agent context (OPN-63).

options.detail: Secrets never enter agent context; an agent cannot publish to a server its host was not configured for.

items.question: How does RichView Publish join the rewrite's architecture, and what happens to the PR #70 stack News runs on until then?
items.why: Decides the component's place in the architecture. Publish is a Git-managed editorial site with its own builder crate, Cloudflare gateway, private R2 releases, a Durable Object ledger, Cloudflare Access and an operator-side publisher. It ran live from its branch until #70 merged into `main` as it is on 2026-10-26 (97ac0d0), and it is mostly JavaScript. Daniel's INT-31 answer builds Publish in the rewrite on a server core shared with RichView Cowork and makes News one Publish instance. PR #70's disposition is D-PUBLISH-PR70 (OPN-14) and News during the rewrite is D-NEWS-DEMO (INT-74); this card records the component outcome and its target architecture.
items.proposed:
**Rebuild in the rewrite on the shared server core; #70 runs News until then.** Publish is built in Rust on the new core: a builder that renders every item through the core's publish contract instead of a second rendering path (ARC-20), and a server on the server core it shares with RichView Cowork (INT-83), which holds storage, identity, enterprise-grade roles and access control managed in a governance section (FEA-SF-19), approvals and the author's quick source edit (INT-26). Roles and approvals live in that server core, never in the core (INT-27). Content lives in its own content repository (ARC-16), and the access, withdrawal and editorial rules of FEA-BR-23 to FEA-BR-30, FEA-BR-44 to FEA-BR-46 and FEA-BR-49 are its requirements. Any Cloudflare adapter is thin and holds no product logic (ARC-03, INT-52). PR #70 is merged into `main` as it is, JavaScript included, so the News work lands and continues (INT-35, INT-52, OPN-14). It is not the rewrite's base: the rewrite carries over its behaviour and decisions, not its code, and ports its JavaScript gateway and desk to Rust when it reaches Publish (INT-49, INT-52). Until the rewrite's Publish serves News, the RichView News session improves News on #70's code and `publish/news` (look, real reports, editor login) on its current JavaScript Worker gateway and owns the operator side: the publisher job, the Access service-token rotation, the bridge credential (re-scoped to 1vecera/richview) and the `publish.yml` validation (OPN-03, OPN-46). news.richview.ai is RichView's own Publish server and always public (ARC-22). Items go public through OPN-54's workflow: an editor's own publish lands private until the editor makes it public, and a submission from an author who isn't an editor goes public automatically once an editor approves it. Live data connectors are standard on Publish as on every RichView server: they come from the connector core RichView builds, which PR #66's work enters; the server holds the data-source credentials, named people manage each connector and access is granted per person (OPN-63, ARC-59, ARC-23, FEA-SF-19). items.title: Data connectors (PR #66)
items.question: Where does PR #66's connector work go: to the Publish track behind a third-party connector engine, or into RichView as its own adapters?
items.why: Daniel's INT-24 answer makes live data a secondary path that belongs to RichView Publish, served by an existing third-party connector engine, with exported data the default for every report. PR #66 built its own adapters instead: it links bundled DuckDB into `richview-app` unconditionally, so the editor, build and bench would compile it, runs MetricFlow through the host's `mf` command, and resolves queries with credentials from a trusted `connectors.toml`. This card decides where that work goes (OPN-63, OPN-10).
items.proposed: **Connector core built by RichView; PR #66's work enters it (D-XPART-CONNECTORS, OPN-63).** Live data connectors are standard on every RichView server, Cowork and Publish, local and hosted. RichView builds the connector core in the rewrite; PR #66's contract (named connectors, bounded read-only queries, bound parameters, snapshots with freshness and provenance; TYP-79, FEA-BR-14 to FEA-BR-16, FEA-BR-43) and code enter it, ported only where they meet the accepted cards (INT-49). Each server offers a set of connectors to set up; named people manage them, and access to each is granted per person under the governance roles (FEA-SF-19). A report block can use SQL against a connector where it would otherwise name a CSV file (TYP-35, TYP-79); the server runs the query and stores a snapshot (FEA-BR-16). Credentials stay in the server's configuration and never appear in `.rmd` files, report folders, rendered output, MCP arguments or agent context (ARC-23). A self-contained HTML file never queries live data; a URL data source is the one exception, which the file downloads when it opens (OPN-63, ARC-11). `richview-core` stays pure and makes no query (ARC-02), and the editor, build and bench do not compile connector engines (ARC-27). Which engines back the connector core, and whether PR #66's DuckDB and MetricFlow adapters are among them, are the agents' technical choice (OPN-63); the DuckDB file-read exposure is closed before any adapter ships (FEA-BR-14). PR #66 itself is closed unmerged (OPN-10).
